clauses.clause: Use a variety of communication modes to share information (C)
clauses.note: Students share information orally through turn-and-talk, partner discussions (Pinky Partners), and the Interactive Word Wall protocol (physical card arrangement + oral explanation). These are primarily oral/spoken modes. While whiteboards are offered as an optional scaffold ('provide white boards and dry-erase markers as an option for students to record (in drawing or writing) their ideas'), the optional nature caps this at partial. The lesson relies predominantly on one mode (oral), with a second mode only optionally available.

verdicts.evidence: Invite students to say out loud what the moon sees on that page and add it to the What the Moon Sees anchor chart.
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to share relevant and accurate information through a variety of different modes (C). Students share relevant, accurate information about what the moon sees at night: during the close viewing, students turn and talk with partners, contributing observations such as "a raccoon; dark, leafy trees" from photographs and videos, and during the read-aloud they "say out loud what the moon sees on that page." These contributions are recorded on the What the Moon Sees anchor chart, and students also share connections during the Interactive Word Wall protocol using sentence frames like "I connected ___ and ___ because they ___." However, the "variety of different modes" clause is only partially met: the dominant mode is oral (turn-and-talk, partner protocols, whole-group sharing), and the only alternative mode—whiteboards for drawing or writing—is offered as an optional scaffold, not a required activity, capping that clause at partial.

verdicts.evidence: 'What do you see in the illustrations that helps you know it is a quiet barnyard?' (Animals are sleeping; the animals are not moving.)
verdicts.rationale: The lesson meets the interpretation (I) clauses: students build and draw from comprehension skills by answering text-dependent questions during the focused read-aloud ("'What do you see in the illustrations that helps you know it is a quiet barnyard?' (Animals are sleeping; the animals are not moving.)") and by observing and describing photographs/videos during close viewing ("'What could the moon 'see' or observe?' (a raccoon; dark, leafy trees)"). These activities have students actively applying comprehension strategies such as using illustrations as evidence, vocabulary acquisition, and close viewing. However, the construction (C) clauses are not met: students do not compose or construct any text in this lesson. The lesson previews that students will write a class narrative poem "beginning in the next lesson," but no drafting, writing, or other composition act occurs here. The standard's (I/C) tag requires both interpretation and construction for full alignment.
